title: Version Control and Reproducibility
summary: Reproducibility, the ability for you or someone else to re-run your analysis and get the same result, is a cornerstone of trustworthy data science, and version control is how you achieve it. Git is a system that tracks changes to your code over time:
content:
# Version Control and Reproducibility ##### final_v2_FINAL_actually_working_2.ipynb An analyst in Pune opened her project folder to hand it over before leaving the company: ``` churn_analysis.ipynb churn_analysis_v2.ipynb churn_analysis_v2_fixed.ipynb churn_analysis_final.ipynb churn_analysis_final_v2.ipynb churn_FINAL_use_this_one.ipynb churn_FINAL_use_this_one_BACKUP.ipynb Copy of churn_FINAL_use_this_one.ipynb ``` Eight files. She could not remember which produced the numbers in the report she had presented six weeks earlier. None had a requirements file. Two of them crashed on cell four because a library had been upgraded since. The handover took nine days and the recipient eventually rebuilt the analysis from scratch. Git solves the file-naming problem, but that is the smallest part. The real problem is **reproducibility** — the ability for you or anyone else to re-run an analysis and get the same result. Without it, your work cannot be verified, extended, audited, or trusted. And in India's increasingly regulated environments, "we cannot reproduce how this model was built" is a compliance finding, not just an inconvenience. ##### Git fundamentals Git tracks changes as a sequence of **commits** — snapshots of your project with a message explaining what changed and why. ```bash git init # start tracking this folder git status # what has changed? git add churn_analysis.py # stage a specific file git add . # stage everything (check .gitignore first!) git commit -m "Add churn feature engineering with tenure bands" git log --oneline --graph --all # see the history git diff # unstaged changes git diff --staged # staged changes ``` The three-stage model confuses people initially: ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Working directory
your edited files] -->|git add| B[Staging area
what will be committed] B -->|git commit| C[Local repository
permanent history] C -->|git push| D[Remote - GitHub] D -->|git pull| C C -->|git checkout| A ``` The staging area exists so you can commit *some* of your changes. If you fixed a bug and also renamed three variables, you can commit those separately with meaningful messages rather than lumping them together. **Commit messages matter more than beginners expect.** `git log` is the only documentation of *why* something changed, and "update" tells your future self nothing. ```bash # Poor git commit -m "update" git commit -m "fixes" git commit -m "asdf" # Good — imperative mood, states what and why git commit -m "Fix leakage: fit scaler inside the pipeline, not before split" git commit -m "Add 7-day rolling features for demand forecast" git commit -m "Drop officer_remark_code: populated post-decision, causes leakage" ``` Commit **small and often**. A commit should be one logical change you could describe in a sentence. Ten focused commits are far easier to review and revert than one enormous one. ##### Branching and merging A branch is an independent line of development. You experiment freely without risking the working version. ```bash git branch # list branches git switch -c feature/add-seasonality # create and switch (modern syntax) # ... make changes, commit them ... git switch main git merge feature/add-seasonality git branch -d feature/add-seasonality # clean up ``` For a solo data science project, a simple pattern works well: `main` always holds a working, reproducible version, and every experiment gets its own branch. If the experiment fails, delete the branch and nothing is lost. If it works, merge it. ```bash git switch -c experiment/try-lightgbm # ... it does not beat the random forest ... git switch main git branch -D experiment/try-lightgbm # discard entirely ``` That workflow removes the fear of breaking working code, which is the actual behavioural benefit of branching. **Merge conflicts** happen when two branches change the same lines. Git marks them in the file: ``` <<<<<<< HEAD n_estimators = 500 ======= n_estimators = 1000 >>>>>>> feature/tune-forest ``` Edit the file to the version you want, delete the marker lines, then `git add` and `git commit`. Conflicts feel alarming the first time and are routine after that. Notebooks conflict horribly, because their JSON contains outputs and execution counts. This is the main reason to strip outputs before committing, covered below. ##### GitHub and remotes ```bash git remote add origin https://github.com/yourname/churn-analysis.git git push -u origin main # first push sets the upstream git push # subsequent pushes git pull # fetch and merge remote changes git clone https://github.com/someone/repo.git # copy an existing repo ``` Beyond backup, GitHub is your professional portfolio. Recruiters and hiring managers look at it, and a repository with a clear README, sensible commit history and reproducible setup signals more than a line on a CV. Two things that raise a repository from "code dump" to "professional": **A commit history that reads as a narrative.** Someone should be able to scan `git log --oneline` and understand how the project developed. **Everything needed to run it, and nothing else.** No 2 GB data files, no `.venv/`, no credentials. ##### .gitignore The file that prevents most Git accidents: ```gitignore # Environments .venv/ venv/ env/ # Python __pycache__/ *.py[cod] .ipynb_checkpoints/ .pytest_cache/ # Secrets — NEVER commit these .env *.key credentials.json config/secrets.yaml # Data — usually too large, sometimes confidential data/raw/ data/processed/ *.csv *.parquet !data/sample/*.csv # exception: small sample data IS useful # Models and outputs models/*.joblib outputs/ *.png # OS and editor cruft .DS_Store Thumbs.db .vscode/ .idea/ ``` Two rules that matter enormously. **Never commit secrets.** An API key pushed to a public repository is scanned and exploited by bots within minutes. And `git rm` does not help — the key remains in the history forever. Removing it properly requires rewriting history with `git filter-repo` and rotating the key regardless. **Do not commit large data.** Git stores every version of every file forever, so a 500 MB CSV committed five times makes a 2.5 GB repository that is painful to clone. Commit a small sample instead, and document where the full data lives. For genuinely large files, `git-lfs` or DVC exist. ##### Reproducible environments Code alone is not enough — the same code with different library versions produces different results, or crashes. ```bash python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate pip install pandas scikit-learn matplotlib pip freeze > requirements.txt ``` ``` # requirements.txt — pinned versions pandas==2.2.3 scikit-learn==1.5.2 matplotlib==3.9.2 numpy==2.1.2 ``` **Pin exact versions.** `pandas>=2.0` means someone installing next year gets pandas 3.2, which may have removed a method you use. `==` guarantees the environment. Anyone can then reproduce it: ```bash python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt ``` Modern tooling handles this more rigorously: ```bash uv init && uv add pandas scikit-learn matplotlib uv sync # installs exactly from uv.lock ``` A lockfile pins transitive dependencies too — not just the packages you asked for, but everything they depend on. Commit the lockfile. Reproducibility also needs **seeds** set everywhere randomness enters: ```python import numpy as np, random, os SEED = 42 random.seed(SEED) np.random.seed(SEED) os.environ["PYTHONHASHSEED"] = str(SEED) # and in every estimator and split train_test_split(X, y, random_state=SEED) RandomForestClassifier(random_state=SEED) ``` An analysis producing a different number every run cannot be verified by anyone, including you. ##### Project structure ``` churn-analysis/ ├── .gitignore ├── .env.example # template — shows what vars are needed, no values ├── README.md ├── requirements.txt ├── data/ │ ├── raw/ # gitignored, immutable, never edited │ ├── processed/ # gitignored, regenerable from raw │ └── sample/ # committed: 500 rows so the repo runs ├── notebooks/ │ ├── 01-eda.ipynb │ ├── 02-feature-engineering.ipynb │ └── 03-modelling.ipynb ├── src/ │ ├── __init__.py │ ├── data.py # loading and cleaning functions │ ├── features.py │ └── model.py ├── tests/ │ └── test_features.py ├── models/ # gitignored └── reports/ └── figures/ ``` The conventions carrying real weight: **numbered notebooks** make the intended order obvious; **`data/raw` is immutable** so you can always start again; **`src/` holds functions promoted out of notebooks** once they stabilise; and **`data/sample/` is committed** so someone cloning the repo can actually run something. `cookiecutter-data-science` scaffolds a version of this in one command and is worth using. ##### Notebooks versus scripts Notebooks are excellent for exploration and problematic for version control and production. | | Notebook | Script | |---|---|---| | Exploration | Excellent | Awkward | | Version control diffs | Terrible (JSON + outputs) | Clean | | Testing | Hard | Easy | | Reuse and import | No | Yes | | Execution order | Whatever you clicked | Top to bottom | The workflow that reconciles them: **explore in notebooks, promote stable code into `src/`, and import it back.** ```python # In the notebook, after adding src/ to the path %load_ext autoreload %autoreload 2 from src.features import build_features, add_tenure_bands df = build_features(raw_df) ``` `autoreload` picks up changes to `src/` without restarting the kernel, which makes this genuinely pleasant rather than a chore. For committing notebooks, strip the outputs: ```bash pip install nbstripout nbstripout --install # runs automatically on every git commit ``` This removes outputs and execution counts before Git sees the file, which makes diffs readable and stops embedded images bloating the repository. And **always run Kernel → Restart and Run All before committing** — if it does not run top to bottom, it is not reproducible, whatever the outputs currently show. ##### The README The README is the front door. Most repositories fail here. ```markdown # Customer Churn Analysis Predicts monthly churn for a subscription business, identifying the onboarding gap that drives 60% of losses. **Key finding:** customers who do not complete onboarding within 30 days churn at 4.1× the baseline rate (n = 12,400). ## Results | Model | ROC-AUC | Recall @ 20% flagged | |---|---|---| | Baseline (majority) | 0.500 | 0.20 | | Logistic regression | 0.781 | 0.54 | | **LightGBM (final)** | **0.834** | **0.67** | ![Feature importance](reports/figures/importance.png) ## Setup ```bash git clone https://github.com/yourname/churn-analysis.git cd churn-analysis python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt ``` ## Reproducing the results ```bash python -m src.data --input data/sample/churn_sample.csv python -m src.model --train --seed 42 ``` Runs in about 90 seconds on a laptop and writes `reports/metrics.json`. ## Data Source: internal subscription database, Jan 2025 – Jun 2026, 84,200 rows. Full data is not committed (confidential). A 500-row anonymised sample is in `data/sample/` and is sufficient to run the pipeline end to end. ## Project structure [tree] ## Limitations - Excludes B2B accounts. - Observational, not experimental — the onboarding effect is correlational. - Assumes 2025–26 behaviour persists; the April 2026 pricing change is not modelled. ``` What makes that work: it states the **finding** before the method, shows **results in a table** so a reader sees the value immediately, gives **copy-pasteable setup commands** that actually work, explains what to do about missing data, and is honest about **limitations**. The test of a good README is simple: could a stranger clone the repository and produce a result within ten minutes, without asking you anything? ##### Common mistakes - No version control at all, managing versions by filename. - Commit messages like "update" and "fixes". - Committing `.venv/`, data files, or model artefacts. - Committing a `.env` file or API key — permanent, even after deletion. - `requirements.txt` with unpinned or missing versions. - No `random_state`, so results change every run. - Notebooks committed with outputs, producing unreadable diffs. - Notebooks that do not run top to bottom. - A README that says only the project name. - No sample data, so nobody can run the repository. ##### Hands-on Take an existing project and initialise Git properly: write a `.gitignore` first, then make several small commits with meaningful messages describing what and why. Create a branch, make an experimental change, and practise both merging it and deleting it. Add a pinned `requirements.txt` and a README. Push to a new GitHub repository. Then do the real test — clone your own repository into a fresh folder, create a new virtual environment from `requirements.txt`, and run it. Whatever breaks is what your reader would have hit. For the mini-project, turn one of your earlier projects into a professional, reproducible GitHub repository. Use the structure above, install `nbstripout`, commit a small sample dataset, set seeds throughout, write a README with results and setup commands, and build a clean commit history. Add one thing most beginner repositories lack: a single command that regenerates your headline result from the sample data. That command is what makes the repository verifiable rather than merely readable. For the assignment, write a README that a stranger could follow to reproduce your results from scratch. Then actually test it — give it to someone else, watch them try, and note every point where they had to guess or ask. Every one of those is a gap in your documentation, and fixing them is the whole exercise. ##### Key takeaways - Git replaces filename versioning with a readable history — commit small, often, and explain *why* in the message. - `.gitignore` before your first commit; secrets and large data committed once stay in the history forever. - Pin exact versions and set seeds everywhere, or the same code produces different results. - Explore in notebooks, promote stable code to `src/`, strip outputs before committing, and restart-and-run-all first. - The README is the front door: state the finding, show results, give working setup commands, and be honest about limitations.
practical_task_reference: Initialize a Git repository for an existing project, make several commits, create and merge a branch, add a requirements.txt and README, and push it all to a new GitHub repository.
mini_project_reference: Take one of your earlier projects and turn it into a professional, reproducible GitHub repository with proper structure, a documented README, pinned dependencies, and a clean commit history.
assignment_reference: Write a README for one of your projects that a stranger could follow to reproduce your results from scratch.
